human_tolerance.notes: Depends on large trees: it nests in the decayed cavities of dead trees, old stumps and softwood live trees, and 'in areas that are extensively deforested, the birds will sometimes utilize gardens, but for the most part they simply will not be present in any numbers'. It does tap on 'aluminum roofs, metal guttering and transformer boxes in urban environments' to make a loud noise. Its excavated cavities are reused by squirrels and bats.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Holds a year-round territory with high site fidelity; a pair begins nesting in April or May and is territorial through the nesting season. Areas around nest sites are marked with drilling holes.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeds once per year, beginning in early May with drumming - slow taps followed by short rapid drumming - to attract a mate. A low 'grr, grr' runs from courtship to the end of the breeding season, and both sexes call, males more.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Both sexes dig the nesting cavity in a dead tree, an old stump or a softwood live tree such as elm, maple or willow; the male locates the hole and seeks his mate's approval by mutual tapping, and the female accepts by completing the excavation. The juvenile is ready to fledge at 24-26 days.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Hides berries and acorns deep in natural crevices to keep them from interspecific competitors.

phases.name: young
phases.note: The juvenile remains in its natal area for about 27 weeks after fledging, and natal dispersal has been observed; it may return to breed there, depending on predation levels and food.

vocalizations.description: The running commentary of the species: a 'churr-churr-churr' or 'thrraa-thrraa-thrraa' with an alternating br-r-r-r-t sound. Red-bellied woodpeckers are noisy birds with many varied calls, and both sexes give them.

About six taps on a hollow tree, a dead limb, or in town on an aluminium roof, a metal gutter or a transformer box. Used from early May to advertise to a mate, and in conflict and pair bonding through bill-drumming; males drum more than females.
A loud repeated 'chee-wuck, chee-wuck, chee-wuck', given in an intraspecific conflict such as two males competing for the same mate, and used to harass an approaching predator.
A low 'grr, grr' exchanged by a pair from the start of courtship until the end of the breeding season.
The high-pitched begging call of a nestling, continued for some time after fledging whenever the young bird sees its parents.

taxonomy.note: The species is monotypic: no subspecies are recognised, so no accepted_id is needed.

external.note: eBird code rebwoo via Wikipedia's infobox.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005); the article adds only 'not globally threatened'.

range.note: Breeds mainly in the eastern United States, as far south as Florida and as far north as Canada. Not treated as introduced anywhere.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'These birds mainly search out arthropods on tree trunks' by drilling and probing bark, and they fly between trees. Ground foraging happens only 'on occasion ... amongst groups of northern flicker woodpeckers', which is why the ground share in habitat.use is 0.05.

traits.nest_type.note: The pair excavates its own cavity in a dead tree, an old stump or a softwood live tree; the same holes serve as roosts, which is why the record's shelter_tag is also cavity.

traits.perching.note: Clings to trunks and branches to work the bark and to hammer stored food into crevices.

traits.lifespan_y.note: A placeholder, and the weakest number in this record: the schema requires a lifespan, and no openly licensed source found for this species gives one. The value is an order-of-magnitude judgement for a medium-sized woodpecker of this size, not a measurement, and should be replaced if a sourced figure turns up.

traits.diet.note: 'These birds mainly search out arthropods on tree trunks. They rarely catch insects in flight. They are omnivores, eating insects, fruits, nuts and seeds', so arthropods take the dominant share at 0.7 and the plant foods split the remaining 0.3 between fruit 0.15 and seed 0.15. The box-nesting wood duck eggs it sometimes takes are a trace and are not carried in the diet fractions.

traits.social.note: 'red-bellied woodpeckers are known to be in monogamous relationships' and hold a year-round territory as a pair.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Diurnal: it forages on trunks by day and roosts in its own cavity at night.

traits.defense.note: 'When approached by a predator, red-bellied woodpeckers either hide from it or harass it with alarm calls. They defend their nests and young aggressively, and may directly attack predators that come near the nest.'

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.4. It drums on suburban roofs and gutters, so it is not shy of built surroundings, but it needs standing dead or softwood trees close by and it harasses rather than approaches a threat near the nest.

habitat.use.note: The strong arboreal share follows 'these birds mainly search out arthropods on tree trunks', with the small ground share covering the occasional foraging with northern flickers.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'The red-bellied woodpecker excavates holes in trees for nesting and roosting', and those cavities are later used by squirrels and bats.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet. Nesting weight is entirely on the excavated cavity; log_pile stands for the dead trees, stumps and snags the article names as nesting and foraging sites, and perch for the trunk and branch surfaces it works and stores food on. Those two shelter weights are authored judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: The article is explicit that the bird depends on large trees, that it is 'simply not present in any numbers' in extensively deforested areas, and that it 'will sometimes utilize gardens'; that sets Adapter rather than Exploiter and the low impervious_max. The drumming on roofs, gutters and transformer boxes shows it will use built structures to make noise. impervious_max, light_max and road_mortality are authored judgement and are not quantified in the source.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Judgement: no open source gives a density. A woodpecker pair holding a year-round territory in mature deciduous forest with snags works on a multi-hectare territory, giving typical 0.15 per hectare, and min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the convention used for turdus-migratorius and cardinalis-cardinalis.

seasonal.strategy.note: A pair 'begins nesting in April or May holding a year-round territory and showing high site fidelity', with no migration described.

seasonal.phases.note: April-May nesting start, once-per-year breeding, the early-May drumming display, the courtship-to-breeding-end 'grr, grr', both-sexes-dig nest excavation in dead trees and stumps and softwood live trees, the male-locates-and-mate-approves courtship, 24-26 days to fledging, crevice storage of berries and acorns, and the juvenile's 27 weeks in the natal area are all stated in the article.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration is authored: 26 days to fledge plus the roughly 27 weeks the juvenile then remains in the natal area gives about 215 days, after which natal dispersal is observed. scale is authored judgement.

vocalizations.note: The churr and thrraa calls, the six-tap drumming on hollow trees and on roofs, gutters and transformer boxes, the loud 'chee-wuck' conflict and harassment call, the low pair 'grr, grr' from courtship to the end of breeding, and the high-pitched 'pree-pree-pree' nestling beg continued after fledging are all quoted or closely paraphrased from the article's Vocalizations, Behavior and ecology and Breeding sections. Cooldowns are authored judgement; no open source quantifies them. No open source gives frequency bands, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Description: mainly light grey face and underparts, black-and-white barring on back, wings and tail, a vivid orange-red cap from bill to nape in the adult male, a red nape patch and a patch above the bill in the female, and a faint reddish tinge on the lower underside. The head is coloured from the pale belly slot so the grey face reads correctly, and the cap and nape parts carry the red; the belly flush uses accent for the tinge that gives the bird its name. The male's full cap is shown. The black-and-white barring is not rendered, which the block model cannot carry. Proportions are authored judgement for a stiff-tailed, long-chisel-billed climber.

behavior.note: Params for the species' own fsm-bark-climber-v1 program, which ships with this record because no shared program fits a bark-working cavity nester. food_m is 3 m because the bird works a single trunk rather than a patch of ground; cover_m 25 m is a hop-between-trees distance; flee_m 10 m and calm_m 25 m bracket the distance at which the bird harasses a threat with alarm calls instead of leaving; cache_tag fruit and the hoard state come from the crevice storage of berries and acorns; drum_m1 and drum_m2 follow the program's declared params and the article's early-May start to breeding.
